theme: “Do justice, love mercy”; God pardons iniquity
readingInstruction: Read Micah 6:1-7:20. God brings a lawsuit against his people, and Micah answers with the most famous summary of the faith in the prophets. Read 6:8 carefully, then enjoy the ending, which is among the loveliest statements of forgiveness in the Bible.
settingTheScene: This final section of Micah is built as a courtroom scene, followed by a lament and a hymn of confidence. God calls the mountains and hills to be the jury, and he asks Israel what he has done to deserve her unfaithfulness. The prophet’s answer to the question of what God requires has become a guide for Christians and Jews alike. The book ends not with judgment but with a song about a God who pardons.
observation: “O my people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Answer me!” (6:3).
“I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery” (6:4).
“With what shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings?” (6:6).
“Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?” (6:7).
“He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (6:8).
“Woe is me! For I have become as when the summer fruit has been gathered” (7:1).
“But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me” (7:7).
“Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love” (7:18).
interpretation:
The lawsuit opens with God’s tender question: “O my people, what have I done to you?” He does not accuse first. He asks. He reminds them of the exodus, of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, and of the story of Balaam. Everything he has done has been for their good. “Remember… that you may know the righteous acts of the LORD.”

The people respond with a panic of religious inflation. What does God want? Burnt offerings? Calves a year old? Thousands of rams, ten thousand rivers of oil? Even their firstborn? The questions escalate toward absurdity. They think that if enough is given, God will be satisfied. This is the religion of bargaining, and it is the opposite of the gospel.

The answer in 6:8 is simple and searching. “He has told you what is good.” It is not a secret. The LORD requires three things. To do justice: to act rightly toward others, especially the weak. To love kindness: the word is the covenant love hesed, loyal, merciful love that we should delight in, not merely practice. And to walk humbly with your God: a life lived in daily company with him, aware of dependence. This is Hosea 6:6 in another form. It is the same heart of the faith.

Chapter 7 begins with grief. Micah feels as if he is alone in a world with no godly person left. Even families are divided. But then comes a great “but as for me.” “I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation.” When the enemy mocks, he says, “Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise.” He accepts the LORD’s discipline because he knows that the LORD will plead his cause.

The book ends with a hymn: “Who is a God like you?” It lists what God does with sin: he pardons iniquity, passes over transgression, does not retain his anger, has compassion, tramples our iniquities underfoot, and casts all our sins into the depths of the sea. He keeps the promise he swore to Abraham and Jacob.
connection: Jesus said the weightier matters of the law are justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23). Hebrews 10:5-10 says that the sacrifices could never take away sins, but the offering of Christ’s body does. In Christ the sins are cast into the sea (Colossians 2:13-14; Hebrews 8:12). Ephesians 2:8-10 says we are saved by grace, created for good works. Romans 12:1 calls us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice.
application:
Memorize Micah 6:8 and take one concrete action today in each of its three parts.

Consider where you are tempted to bargain with God, as the people did.

Thank God that your sins are cast into the depths of the sea. Say it aloud.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what it looks like for you to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly this week.
Thank him that he pardons iniquity.
Ask him to teach you to do this out of love and not to earn his love.
